phonemes.desc: Short close back rounded [u], held brief — the u of Old Norse is a true short vowel, not the long ú; closer to the vowel of English 'put' than of 'pool'.
The long (geminate) dental-alveolar lateral [lː], held audibly as in modern Icelandic Ullur — the one articulatory event the double letter records.
The nominative masculine ending -r (from older *-z), a tapped or trilled [r] closing the single syllable; in later Icelandic it fused with the l, but the reconstructed form keeps it sounded.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ULL-r' — one firm beat, the vowel short and rounded as in 'pull', the double l held a fraction long, and the final r sounded; as in modern Icelandic Ullur.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Ullr, son of Sif and stepson of Thor; the name is attested for the god and in a handful of compound personal names, but is rare as a human name.

kin.label: Proto-Germanic
kin.form: *wulþuz, 'glory, splendor' — compare Gothic wulþus 'glory' and Old English wuldor, the word behind 'Wuldorfæder', Glory-Father, in the biblical poems.

kin.label: Latin
kin.form: Ollerus — Saxo Grammaticus's Latinization of the name in the Gesta Danorum.

kin.label: Modern Scandinavian
kin.form: Ull (Norwegian and Swedish), living above all in the map: Ullensaker, Ullern, Ullevi, Ullensvang and their dozens of kin.

pronunciation.note: Ullr is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. Only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input; the tier says something about orthography and nothing about the god.

domains.title: Archery, Hunting, Skiing
domains.subtitle: The Snowshoe God of the Yew-Dales
domains.lead: Ullr, son of Sif and stepson of Thor, dwells in Ýdalir — the Yew-Dales, named for the tree that gave the North its bows — and he is everything the address promises: a bowman so good and a skier so swift that no one can compete with him, fair of face, with a warrior's skill, the god it is good to call on in single combat. The Edda gives him a paragraph; the map gives him a province. Scores of holy places across Norway and Sweden — Ullensaker, Ullevi, Ullern — still bear his name, the fossil of a cult far older and greater than his surviving verses, and a Danish chronicler remembered a rumor that once, for ten years, this god ruled heaven itself in Odin's place.

cards.name: The Yew Bow
cards.desc: The bow of Ýdalir timber — Snorri calls Ullr a bowman so good that no one can compete with him, and his hall's own name advertises the wood of northern bows.

cards.name: The Snowshoes
cards.desc: Öndurr, the snowshoe or ski: the skalds knew Ullr as öndur-Áss, the Snowshoe God, and Saxo remembered Ollerus gliding across the sea on a spell-marked bone.

cards.name: The Shield-Ship
cards.desc: Skaldic verse calls the shield 'Ullr's ship', and Snorri lists shield-god among his heiti — behind the kenning stands a lost story of the god travelling on his shield.

cards.name: The Oath-Ring
cards.desc: In Atlakviða, Guðrún reminds Atli of oaths once sworn 'by the ring of Ullr' — the god's name stamped on the holiest metal in the hall, proof of a legal weight the myths no longer explain.

symbols.name: The yew bow
symbols.meaning: The weapon of Ýdalir timber — archery as divine craft, and the hall's name as the god's own advertisement

symbols.name: The snowshoes
symbols.meaning: Öndurr, the ski or snowshoe — winter travel raised to godhead; the kenning öndur-Áss, Snowshoe God

symbols.name: The shield, 'Ullr's ship'
symbols.meaning: The skaldic kenning that makes his shield a vessel — a fragment of a lost voyage myth

symbols.name: The oath-ring
symbols.meaning: The holy ring of Atlakviða by which the deepest oaths were sworn — Ullr as guarantor of sworn speech

symbols.name: Ýdalir
symbols.meaning: The Yew-Dales, his hall in Grímnismál's survey of heaven — one of the few divine addresses the poems give

symbols.name: The yew tree
symbols.meaning: Taxus baccata, the bow-wood of the North — the living emblem of his nameless cult landscape

mythology.lead: Ullr's dossier is a paradox: among the best-attested gods in the Scandinavian place-name record and among the least narrated in the literature. The Poetic Edda gives him a stanza and a half; Snorri gives him a paragraph and a list of kennings; Saxo gives him a throne for ten years. What the myths withhold, the map supplies — a god whose story was carved into the landscape of Norway and Sweden long before anyone wrote an Edda.

myths.title: The Yew-Dales
myths.text:
In Grímnismál's numbered survey of the gods' dwellings, the fifth hall belongs to Ullr: Ýdalir heita þar er Ullr hefir sér of görva sali — 'Yew-Dales is the name of the place where Ullr has made himself a hall.' The poem gives him no lineage, no wife, no adventure — only an address. But what an address: the yew is the bow-wood of the North, and a god who halls himself in its dales declares his office in the naming.

Grímnismál touches him once more at its close, when the tortured Geirrøðr's son is blessed at the fire: Ullar hylli hefr ok allra goða — 'the favor of Ullr and of all the gods shall he have.' In a poem where Odin alone speaks, Ullr's name stands first among the gods whose goodwill is invoked — a small, unexplained precedence that commentators have never stopped noticing.

myths.title: The Snowshoe God
myths.text:
Snorri's whole account of Ullr is one packed sentence: 'One is called Ullr, son of Sif and stepson of Thor. He is such a good bowman and so fast on skis that no one can compete with him. He is also fair of face and has a warrior's accomplishments. It is good to call on him in single combat.' Son of Sif, raised in Thor's household of Thrúðheimr, the god of the bow, the ski, and the duel — Snorri compresses a cult into a catalogue.

Skáldskaparmál keeps the poets' shorthand: Ullr may be called son of Sif, kinsman of Thor, the Snowshoe God, the Bow God, the Hunting God, the Shield God. And the shield, the skalds agreed, is 'Ullr's ship' — a kenning Snorri preserves without its story. Somewhere behind the verse stands a lost myth in which the god travelled on his shield as on a vessel; the words survived the tale.

myths.title: The Ring of Ullr
myths.text:
When Atli has betrayed the Burgundian kings and Guðrún turns on him, she recalls the oaths he swore long before: by the sun and the south-facing sun-hall, by Sigtyr's mount — and at Ullar hringi, 'by the ring of Ullr'. The oath-ring, the holy arm-ring of the temple on which the deepest vows were sworn, is here named as Ullr's own.

Nothing else in the corpus explains the attribution. A bow-god with a cult-ring suggests something the myths never spell out: a god of the thing, the assembly, the sworn word — a legal weight that matches the strange priority Grímnismál gives him. The line is one stanza long, and it has carried whole theories of Ullr as an ancient god of law and sky, older than the family of gods the Edda finally recorded.

myths.title: Ollerus on the Throne
myths.text:
Saxo Grammaticus, euhemerizing the gods as ancient kings and wizards, keeps the one adventure the Icelanders forgot. When Othinus was driven into exile for dishonoring the public cult, the gods 'not wishing Odin to drive public religion into exile with him' put one Ollerus — the Latin form of Ullr — in his place. For ten years Ollerus bore the name and the rites of Odin and ruled at Uppsala; when the true Odin returned, the usurper was driven out, fled to Sweden, and was slain by the Danes as he tried to rebuild his glory in a new land.

Saxo adds the rumor (fama est) that Ollerus was such a cunning wizard that he could cross the seas on a bone he had marked with terrible spells — a detail readers have long recognized as the winter-god's equipment refracted through a Danish chronicler's Latin: the enchanted bone is the ski or skate, and the sea it crosses is the snowfield. A god who can wear Odin's name for a decade is no minor figure; Saxo's fable reads like the last echo of an age when Ullr stood nearer the center of heaven than the Edda dares admit.

lore.syncretism: Ullr's true comparison class is not another mythology's gods but his own name's reach. Inside the corpus his nearest kin is [[skadi|Skaði]], the other ski-going hunter of the northern corpus, and the skalds' pairing of bow, snowshoe, and shield makes him the Æsir's winter counterpart to the Vanir she married into. His mythic position — son of [[sif|Sif]], stepson of [[thor|Thor]] — seats him in the one household of the gods Snorri trusted with a family tree, and Saxo's Ollerus, ruling in [[odinn|Óðinn]]'s place at Uppsala, keeps a memory that this 'minor' god once carried major authority. Beyond the corpus, the old etymological tie to Proto-Germanic *wulþuz, 'glory' — Gothic wulþus, Old English wuldor — led generations of scholars to see in Ullr a faded sky- or splendor-god, and the third-century Thorsberg chape inscription owlþuþewaz may carry his name-element centuries before the Eddas. Nineteenth-century comparatists reached for bow-bearing Apollo and other Indo-European hunters; current handbooks are cooler. Simek and Lindow emphasize what can actually be shown: a cult dense in Norway and Sweden, absent from Denmark and Iceland, a ring-oath and a hall, and a name meaning 'Glory' — the profile of a god whose importance peaked before our sources were written.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ullr's afterlife is the snow itself. When Scandinavia reinvented skiing in the nineteenth century as sport and national emblem, the old snowshoe god was waiting: Norwegian ski culture embraced Ull as its patron, and his name has crowned winter festivals, ski clubs, and slopes ever since — the only Norse god whose modern cult is conducted on mountains with equipment. The name lives on as a Scandinavian given name and, far more densely, in the map: Ullensaker, Ullern, Ullensvang, Ullevi and their kin keep his sanctuaries' names long after the sanctuaries fell. Modern Heathen and Ásatrú communities call on him for winter sport and for the sworn word, reading the oath-ring of Atlakviða as seriously as the bow. And in the broader reception he stands as the textbook case of a great god the literature lost — the figure every handbook uses to prove that the Edda's silence is not a cult's measure.
lore.extendedMeditation: Every tradition in the lexicon has its quiet god, the one the myths barely use and cannot forget. Ullr is the North's. Grímnismál names his hall among the first of heaven's addresses and puts his favor first among the gods' blessings; the poets swear by his ring; the map of two countries is salted with his holy places — and Snorri, who can spend pages on a fishing trip, gives him one sentence. The discrepancy is itself the record. Whatever Ullr was at the height of his worship — bow-god, sky-god, lord of the sworn oath, the Glory his name still means — it belonged to an older layer of the religion than the Eddas preserve, and by the thirteenth century only the specialists kept the tokens: a stanza, a kenning, a rumor from Denmark that he once sat in Odin's seat. Ullr teaches the reader of myth a hard and useful lesson: the silence of a source is evidence about the source, never about the god. The yew-dales are still on the map.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Ullr — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚢᛚᛚᚱ (u-l-l-r). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: ullr.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

sources.name: Poetic Edda: Grímnismál 5 (Ýdalir, the hall Ullr made for himself) and 42 (Ullar hylli, the favor of Ullr invoked first among the gods); Atlakviða 30 (the oath sworn 'by the ring of Ullr'), trans. Carolyne Larrington

Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 31 (Ullr son of Sif, stepson of Thor; the bowman, the skier, the god of single combat); Skáldskaparmál (kennings: the Snowshoe God, the Bow God, the Hunting God, the Shield God; the shield as 'Ullr's ship'), trans. Anthony Faulkes
Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum, Book 3 (Ollerus rules in Othinus's place for ten years; the spell-marked bone; driven out and slain in Sweden), trans. Peter Fisher, ed. Hilda Ellis Davidson

lore.archaeology: Ullr's archaeology is written across two countries rather than buried in any one of them: no image and no votive hoard can be securely assigned to him, but the Scandinavian place-name record is the densest of any god outside the great three. Norway keeps Ullensaker ('Ullr's field'), Ullern ('Ullr's meadow' or from Ullarvin), Ullensvang, and the lost Ullarhof; Sweden keeps Ullevi and Lilla Ullevi ('Ullr's sanctuary'), Ulleråker ('Ullr's field'), Ullvi and their kin — a cult landscape spread across south-eastern Norway and eastern middle Sweden, with not one secure Ullr-name in Denmark or Iceland. At Lilla Ullevi in Bro parish, Uppland, excavations in the 2000s uncovered an Iron Age cult building rich in amulet rings — a rare look at the kind of site the name advertises, though the identification with the god rests on the place-name alone. The oldest possible attestation is runic and continental: the third-century Thorsberg shield-chape (Schleswig) reads owlþuþewaz, whose first element is the *wulþu- 'glory' that became the name Ullr — whether theonym or personal name is disputed, but it proves the name's antiquity. Later antiquarian tradition supplied the familiar image: seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Icelandic paper manuscripts (the 'Edda oblongata' type) picture Ullr on skis with his bow — an early modern reconstruction, not a medieval witness.
